definition: A simple auxiliary classifier trained on a model's internal representations to test whether specific information (like syntactic structure) is encoded in those representations.
details: Probing classifiers are a common interpretability research tool for investigating what kinds of linguistic or semantic knowledge different layers of a language model have learned to encode.

explainer.lead: A simple auxiliary classifier trained on a model's internal representations to test whether specific information is encoded there. It matters because it reveals what a model has learned to represent without relying on its outputs.

tiers.eli5: You attach a tiny quiz to a hidden layer to see if the information you care about is written there.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers train lightweight classifiers per layer to localize knowledge such as syntax or entities; a pitfall is that a high probe score may reflect the probe's own capacity rather than clean encoding.
tiers.paperLevel: Fit a simple classifier on frozen activations to predict a target property; limits are that probe accuracy is correlational and does not establish causal use by the model.

explainer.example: A linear probe on layer 6 activations of a language model predicts part-of-speech tags with high accuracy, suggesting syntactic information is present there.
